name: Water

bonding.summary: Two polar O–H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen but pulls them closer (Δχ 1.24), leaving O partly negative and each H partly positive. Its two lone pairs push the hydrogens together to 104.5°, and the δ+ hydrogens of one molecule cling to the lone pairs of the next: hydrogen bonds.

occurrence: Covers 71% of Earth's surface; found as ice across the Solar System.
facts: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold its molecules in an open lattice.
Water's boiling point would be near −80 °C without hydrogen bonding.
summary: Water is small but strongly polar, so its molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds, giving it its unusual high boiling point and floating ice.

name: Hydrogen peroxide

bonding.summary: A weak O–O single bond with an H on each oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Each oxygen shares pairs with H and the other O and keeps two lone pairs. Lone-pair repulsion makes the O–O bond weak and the molecule twisted.

formation: H2 + O2 -> H2O2 (anthraquinone process, via a catalyst)
occurrence: Made in cells and industry; in the atmosphere in small amounts.
facts: Your cells make hydrogen peroxide and destroy it with the enzyme catalase, which makes it fizz on cuts.
hazards: Concentrated solutions are corrosive and can explode with organics.
summary: H2O2 is like water with an extra oxygen; its weak O–O bond makes it a strong oxidizer and bleach.

name: Hydrogen chloride

bonding.summary: One polar H–Cl bond; in water it gives up H+ completely.
bonding.electronSharing: Chlorine pulls the shared pair toward itself (Δχ 0.96) and keeps three lone pairs. In water the bond breaks unevenly: Cl keeps both electrons as Cl−, and H+ joins water as H3O+.

occurrence: Volcanic gases and your stomach (dilute hydrochloric acid).
facts: Stomach acid is about 0.1 M hydrochloric acid, pH 1.5–3.5.
summary: HCl is a polar gas that becomes a strong acid in water.

name: Hydrogen fluoride

bonding.summary: The most polar single bond between two nonmetals; strong hydrogen bonding.
bonding.electronSharing: Fluorine pulls the shared pair very strongly (Δχ 1.78). The strong bond means HF releases H+ only partly in water, so it is a weak acid.

facts: HF is a weak acid yet dissolves glass, because fluoride bonds strongly to silicon.
hazards: Extremely dangerous: it penetrates skin and binds calcium in tissue.
summary: HF is a weak but very hazardous acid that can etch glass.

name: Hydrogen bromide

bonding.summary: A polar single bond, longer and weaker than H–Cl.
bonding.electronSharing: Bromine pulls the pair toward itself and keeps three lone pairs. The weaker bond makes HBr a stronger acid than HCl.

facts: Among HF, HCl, HBr and HI, acid strength rises as the bond gets longer and weaker.
summary: HBr is a strong acid in water, stronger than hydrochloric acid.

name: Hydrogen iodide

bonding.summary: The longest and weakest hydrogen-halogen bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Iodine and hydrogen pull on the pair almost equally (Δχ 0.46), but the long, weak bond breaks easily in water.

facts: HI is the strongest of the hydrohalic acids.
summary: HI is the strongest of the halogen acids because its bond is the weakest.

name: Hydrogen sulfide

bonding.summary: Like water, but with weaker polarity and almost no hydrogen bonding.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur shares one pair with each H and keeps two lone pairs. With Δχ only 0.38, the bonds are barely polar, so H2S is a gas, unlike water.

occurrence: Volcanoes, swamps, sewers and natural gas.
facts: You can smell H2S at 0.5 parts per billion, but high levels deaden the sense of smell.
hazards: Highly toxic despite its warning smell.
summary: H2S is the rotten-egg gas: water's chemical cousin, but a deadly gas.

name: Sulfuric acid

bonding.summary: Sulfur at the center of a tetrahedron of four oxygens, two carrying hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur shares electrons with four oxygens; the two O–H groups give up H+ easily because the electron-hungry SO2 group pulls electrons away from them.

occurrence: Made in larger amounts than any other chemical; also in Venus's clouds.
facts: Industrial output of sulfuric acid was once used as a measure of a country's industrial strength.
hazards: Severely corrosive; dehydrates tissue and releases great heat with water.
summary: Sulfuric acid is the world's most-produced industrial chemical.

name: Nitric acid

bonding.summary: A flat molecule: N bonded to three oxygens, one carrying the hydrogen.
bonding.electronSharing: The two terminal N–O bonds share a delocalized π pair (resonance). Nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and one oxygen a negative one.

occurrence: Synthetic; traces form from lightning in rain.
facts: Mixed with hydrochloric acid it makes aqua regia, which dissolves gold.
summary: Nitric acid is a strong oxidizing acid used mainly to make fertilizers and explosives.

name: Phosphoric acid

bonding.summary: Phosphorus in a tetrahedron of oxygens, three bearing hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: The P=O group pulls electrons away from the three O–H groups so they can release H+ one at a time.

formation: Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 -> 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4 + HF (wet process)
facts: The tang in cola drinks comes from phosphoric acid.
summary: Phosphoric acid is a mild acid in food and a major route to fertilizers.

name: Carbonic acid

bonding.summary: A carbon bonded to one C=O and two O–H groups, all flat.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O double bond pulls electrons and helps the O–H groups release H+. In water it falls apart into CO2 and H2O almost as fast as it forms.

occurrence: In fizzy drinks, rain and blood, always in tiny amounts.
facts: Pure carbonic acid was only isolated as a solid in 1993 and as a gas in 2011.
summary: Carbonic acid forms when CO2 dissolves in water; it makes soda tangy and buffers your blood.

name: Ammonia

bonding.summary: Three N–H bonds and one lone pair, forming a low pyramid.
bonding.electronSharing: Nitrogen shares one pair with each hydrogen and pulls them closer. Its lone pair sits on top and can grab an H+, which is why ammonia is a base.

formation: N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3 (Haber–Bosch, iron catalyst, about 450 °C and 200 atm)
occurrence: Made in huge amounts; also from decaying organic matter.
facts: Fertilizer from the Haber–Bosch process feeds roughly half of the world's population.
summary: Ammonia is the base of modern agriculture: most nitrogen in your body passed through a Haber–Bosch plant.

name: Sodium hydroxide (lye)

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and OH− ions held by ionic attraction; the O–H inside the ion is covalent.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives its 3s electron away entirely. The hydroxide ion keeps that extra electron, shared between O and H.

formation: 2 NaCl + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2 + Cl2 (chlor-alkali process)
facts: Dissolving NaOH in water releases enough heat to make the water boil.
hazards: Severely caustic to skin and eyes.
summary: Lye is a strong base made from salt water, used to make soap and paper.

name: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions and two OH− ions per formula unit.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons away; each hydroxide holds one extra electron.

occurrence: Made by adding water to quicklime.
facts: Lime mortar hardens by slowly absorbing CO2 from the air and turning back into limestone.
summary: Slaked lime has been used in building mortar for thousands of years; it decomposes at 580 °C instead of melting.

name: Boric acid

bonding.summary: Boron bonded to three OH groups in a flat triangle.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron has only three valence electrons, all used in B–O bonds, leaving an empty orbital. It acts as an acid by accepting OH− from water rather than giving away H+.

facts: Its flat molecules stack in layers held by hydrogen bonds, making the crystals slippery.
hazards: Mildly toxic if swallowed in quantity.
summary: Boric acid is a weak acid that works by accepting hydroxide ions instead of releasing protons.
